facts.claim: The table recommends short/long pairs of the same vowel quality. Short e, i, o, u, y are tense in that table; section19 expressly accepts the traditional lax short values as a practical English-speaker substitute. This permission does not erase the distinction between a recommended classroom reading and a detailed reconstruction.
facts.teaching_recommendation: Choose and state one practical convention. Traditional bet/bit/foot and rounded-short-o cues are authorized by section19; do not say that every practical pair differs only in duration if the short member is taught lax.

facts.claim: Short æ and long ǣ have the same open-front quality in Fulk’s table. The macron marks a real meaning-distinguishing length difference.
facts.teaching_recommendation: Use cat or bat for æ and hold that same quality for ǣ. This follows Fulk’s explicit value; Cook’s care cue should not be recycled for rhotic American speakers.

facts.claim: The front rounded vowel y has no ordinary native English equivalent. Section12 derives the long/tensed quality by maintaining the tongue posture of ee while rounding the lips for oo.
facts.teaching_recommendation: Supply a mouth-position instruction. Short rounded bit is compatible with the optional lax-short-vowel convention; long rounded beet is the source’s explicit high-front-round target. Do not teach modern consonantal y or replace both qualities silently with ordinary i.

facts.claim: Fulk adopts short ea/eo/ie = [æu, eu, iu] and long ēa/ēo/īe = [æːu, eːu, iːu], acknowledging scholarly disagreement. Each is one syllable; the long first element is held longer. The second element retains rounding.
facts.teaching_recommendation: For a coherent source-based guide, choose Fulk’s rounded-glide convention explicitly. Describe a single smooth movement toward oo without a second beat; do not equate any of these with an exact modern American diphthong.

facts.claim: The earlier West Saxon unstressed vowels should remain distinguishable. Fulk recommends unstressed e approximating a light bet vowel rather than reducing every ending to modern English uh. Certain syllabic-resonant spellings are a bounded exception.
facts.teaching_recommendation: Keep final and unstressed vowels audible and differentiated. A beginner does not need the reconstruction of syllabic resonants.

facts.claim: Some ea/eo spellings contain a silent e that marks the preceding consonant’s palatal value rather than a diphthong. Fulk marks such e with an underdot.
facts.teaching_recommendation: State that the vowel-letter rules have lexical exceptions and supply the pronunciation of any such example actually used. Cook does not supply Fulk’s underdots, so do not make dotted spelling a prerequisite for reading course text.

facts.claim: Thorn and eth do not distinguish the two th sounds. Fulk’s ordinary rule voices f, s, þ/ð between voiced sounds and leaves them voiceless initially, finally, or next to a voiceless consonant. Historical stress and word-formation boundaries create exceptions.
facts.teaching_recommendation: Use knife/knives only to illustrate a documented alternation, not as a claim that Modern English predicts every word. Give any needed prefix/compound exception locally. Choose Fulk’s rule openly instead of combining it with Cook’s broader syllable-final voicing rule.

facts.claim: A doubled consonant has additional duration; Fulk compares nn with the n spanning pen-knife.
facts.teaching_recommendation: Use a cross-word or compound boundary cue such as pen-knife, with no extra vowel. For stops, hold the closure longer rather than adding a second syllable.

facts.claim: c and g have several values; the front-vowel tendency is not a complete rule from the written neighboring vowel. Historical changes and following back vowels account for lexical and inflectional exceptions. Fulk’s overpoints explicitly distinguish the selected values.
facts.teaching_recommendation: Give the common k/ch and hard-g/y/continuous-g sounds, then qualify spelling tendencies and supply specific examples. Do not silently add overpoints throughout the existing Cook-based text or claim every c/g next to e, i, y is palatal.

facts.claim: Ordinary unpalatalized ng includes the g of finger. Palatal ng can have the end of singe, as in senġan. Most cg/gg is the bridge-type affricate, but frogga/frocga and docga have stops, and a few compound junctures preserve different sound sequences.
facts.teaching_recommendation: Avoid the absolute statement ng is always as in finger. For a small guide give finger as the ordinary pattern and singe as a supplied exception; avoid an independently tested complete reconstruction of ng.

facts.claim: sc generally has the sh sound but sk remains in specified environments, including frosc. Fulk prints sċ for sh and sc for sk. Inflection can change the selected sound, as with frosc/frosċes.
facts.teaching_recommendation: Use ship as the ordinary cue and give a bounded sk example. State usually rather than always.

facts.claim: h is ordinary h syllable-initially and a continuous back-of-mouth fricative elsewhere; g has a voiced counterpart of that fricative in ordinary nonpalatal medial/final environments. Fulk does not mark front/back allophones in the basic table.
facts.teaching_recommendation: Use hat for initial h and plain mouth instructions for the absent English fricatives. Cook’s ach/ich distinction can supply a bounded front/back articulation note. The continuous g is made at the hard-g place without full closure and with voice; it is neither an ordinary English g stop nor a silent letter.

facts.claim: The IPA introduction uses r as in run and p/t/k as in span/store/score. The inspected Old English sound chapter supplies no separate requirement to trill r or detailed aspiration prescription.
facts.teaching_recommendation: Do not attribute mandatory rolled r to Fulk. If using span/store/score to illustrate small-puff stops, label the plain-language cue as an editorial aid and keep it peripheral.

facts.claim: Fulk gives x as [xs] with later [ks]; Cook §7 gives hs as modern English x.
facts.teaching_recommendation: A k+s reading can be adopted as Cook’s practical/later convention, but do not label it Fulk’s only or earliest value.

facts.claim: Most words have initial stress. ge- is unstressed, be-/for- almost always so, and verb prefixes generally leave primary stress on the root. Denominal verbs can retain prefix stress. Function-word and prefix macrons are partly editorial conventions despite actual unstressed shortening.
facts.teaching_recommendation: Teach a short stress rule plus supplied exceptions. Distinguish stress from length. A careful reading exercise may follow printed macrons, but a claim that every printed macron was always equally long in connected speech would exceed Fulk’s account.

facts.claim: Fulk distinguishes short a before nasal consonants, with a rounded bought-type quality, from the father-type value elsewhere.
facts.teaching_recommendation: Choose explicitly whether to teach this nasal condition or retain a simpler Cook-based uniform father-type classroom a. Do not label the latter Fulk’s exact complete vowel system.

comparisons.cook: Cook §5 p7 uses men, fin, broad shortened, full and rounded i of it for short e/i/o/u/y.
comparisons.fulk: Fulk §19 pp13–14 prefers tense short values in reconstruction but explicitly accepts these traditional lax classroom values.
comparisons.decision: Compatible practical option if its approximate status is stated.

comparisons.cook: Cook §5 p7 gives the dialect-bound English cue care.
comparisons.fulk: Fulk §16 p11 explicitly gives the same quality as short æ, held longer.
comparisons.decision: Use held cat/bat by explicit choice of Fulk; do not claim American care has that value.

comparisons.cook: Cook §5 p7 has ea = æ + uh, ēa = ē + ah, eo = e + o, ēo = ē + o, ie = i + ĕh, īe = ī + ĕh; his opening note makes the second element very slight. The easily misread ē in the long ēa row was independently checked at300dpi by the Cook auditor.
comparisons.fulk: Fulk §§16/20 pp12/14 deliberately adopts rounded æu/eu/iu and long-first-element counterparts.
comparisons.decision: Substantive difference. Choose one convention openly; recommend Fulk’s systematic scheme for the guide.

comparisons.cook: Cook §8 pp8–9 includes voicing after a sonant at syllable end.
comparisons.fulk: Fulk §17 p12 restricts the ordinary voiced environment to between voiced sounds, leaving word-final fricatives voiceless and adding historical-stress/compound exceptions.
comparisons.decision: Substantive difference. Recommend Fulk and disclose the departure from Cook.

comparisons.cook: Cook §7 p8 permits nearly modern English r/l and explicitly retains h in hl/hn/hr/hw and w in wr/wl.
comparisons.fulk: Fulk basic IPA table uses run; no mandatory trill or explicit voiceless-sonorant instruction was found in §§9–23.
comparisons.decision: Use Cook’s practical sounded-cluster instruction; do not invent a sourced requirement for rolled r.

comparisons.cook: Cook §10 p9 states broad tendencies with exceptions but does not overpoint c/g.
comparisons.fulk: Fulk §§18/135 uses overpoints and underpoints to expose complex lexical distinctions.
comparisons.decision: Retain Cook orthography and give local help. Removing Fulk’s dots is an explicit typographic normalization, not evidence that Cook prints the same vowel spelling.

editorial_cue_limits: The official Fulk sound table calls its English comparisons approximate. It does not discuss General American mergers or accent variation.
Avoid man as the main æ cue because American nasal raising can change it; cat/bat is an editorial substitution.
Bait/boat often glide in American English; steady ē/ō instructions are editorial explanations of the selected monophthong targets.
Bought/law do not distinguish a rounded short-o target for cot–caught-merged speakers; provide a rounded-mouth instruction, or select a different clearly stated practical value.
Father is a useful approximate a/ā cue, but duration must be stated independently of English spelling.
Unfamiliar sounds need tongue/lip/airflow instructions; a foreign-language word alone does not meet the user’s needs.
The technical audit includes IPA for precision; the learner guide should not inherit its transcription density.
normalization_policy: Source examples in facts retain Fulk overpoints, underpoints, thorn and vowel spelling, normalized to UnicodeNFC only.
If a guide example removes ċ/ġ/sċ overpoints or ẹ underpoints, record that exact change and supply the relevant pronunciation.
Do not silently change Fulk y/i/e to match a Cook headword or convert þ to ð without recording the selected surface.
No exercises from Fulk §§13–14,24 or136 are assigned by this source audit.
proposed_coordinator_resolution: Close the source audit when the coordinator accepts the inspected evidence; settle the learner reading convention in the pronunciation contract before prose. No blocking source-access uncertainty remains for the bounded scope.
